Démocrite d'Abdère, à la suite de son ma: Democritus of Abdera, following his teacher Leucippus, claims that everything is made of tiny, indivisible particles moving in the void: atoms, from the Greek atomos, “uncuttable.” With no experiment to show it, it is a philosophical intuition. It took John Dalton, around 1808, for an atomic theory based on measurements, then Einstein (1905) and Jean Perrin (1908) for atoms to become indisputable.
Démocrite a eu raison 2 300 ans trop tôt: Democritus was right 2,300 years too early. In science, that's almost worse than being wrong.
Démocrite imaginait des atomes insécable: Democritus imagined unbreakable atoms, hooked or smooth, of all shapes. There are a hundred and eighteen kinds, and none is unbreakable. A wild atom comes out of the void to tell him so.
Lavoisier et la masse qui se conserve: Lavoisier and the conservation of mass
Antoine Lavoisier publie le Traité éléme: Antoine Lavoisier published the Elementary Treatise on Chemistry. By weighing everything, before and after each reaction, he showed that mass is conserved. He explained combustion by oxygen and buried the phlogiston theory. His wife, Marie-Anne Paulze, translated English works, kept the laboratory notebooks and engraved the treatise's plates.
« Rien ne se perd, rien ne se crée » : L: “Nothing is lost, nothing is created”: Lavoisier didn't write that sentence word for word. But you don't lose this turn.
Lavoisier était aussi fermier général, c: Lavoisier was also a tax farmer, that is, a tax collector. Arrested during the Terror, he was guillotined on May 8, 1794. The phrase attributed to the judge, “The Republic has no need of scientists,” is probably a legend: he most likely never said it. Lagrange is said to have remarked that it took only an instant to cut off that head, and a hundred years might not be enough to produce another like it.
Retour au début de l'époque. Vous gardez: Back to the start of the era. You keep your head, which is already better than Lavoisier.
Dmitri Mendeleïev range les 63 éléments: Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the 63 known elements by mass and properties, and left empty squares for unknown elements whose properties he predicted. Gallium (1875), scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) came to fill them. According to a story he told himself, the table came to him in a dream.
63 éléments connus en 1869, 63 cases ici: 63 elements known in 1869, 63 squares here. Coincidence? Yes. The AI is not superstitious.
Mendeleïev laisse des cases vides pour d: Mendeleev left empty squares for elements not yet known, and predicted their properties. Gallium proved him right in 1875. An atom comes out of its square.
Marie et Pierre Curie découvrent le polo: Marie and Pierre Curie discovered polonium, named after Marie's native Poland, then radium. Marie Curie was the first woman Nobel laureate (physics, 1903) and remains the only person awarded in two different sciences (chemistry, 1911). Her notebooks are still radioactive: the Bibliothèque nationale de France keeps her manuscripts in lead-lined boxes.
Ses carnets sont radioactifs depuis plus: Her notebooks have been radioactive for more than a century. Your revision notes have a half-life of about two days.
Marie et Pierre Curie traitent des tonne: Marie and Pierre Curie processed tons of pitchblende to isolate a few decigrams of radium. Here, one wild atom will do.
